note: Declared cross-runtime / cross-host acceptance criteria (feature 109 US1, FR-001).
A criterion listed here is one whose CLAIM spans more than one runtime, host or
implementation. Feature 109 exists because such criteria were previously discharged by
running ONE participant: on 2026-09-04 feature 101 was recorded implemented with the exact
C# lines named in CLAUDE.md and docs/known-issues.md, those lines were still defective, and
the Gleam half had shipped with no test file at all -- invisible, because nothing in the
566-check suite had ever started a second runtime.
SC-001 baseline, recorded 2026-09-06: the count of declared multi-participant criteria was 0.

criteria.title: Dart and C# accept and refuse the same goal terms, byte for byte
criteria.requirement: feature 101 FR-008 / SC-003 -- the same goal text must be accepted or refused IDENTICALLY across runtimes
why_differential: A per-runtime pattern assertion passes while the two runtimes disagree about WHICH
variable bound or WHAT the refusal said. Only a transcript comparison can fail on that.
Gleam is a declared non-participant HERE and is pinned in-language instead, at
because the Gleam REPL does not offer this script's `load` surface. That is a declared,
tested division of the obligation -- not a silent gap.

participants.name: dart
participants.why: the reference implementation of the goal-term front end; every other runtime is a port of it

freshness.why: the runner prefers the compiled kernel snapshot .dart_tool/repl.dill whenever it exists, and a snapshot older than lib/ or bin/ answers for code that is no longer the code. Omitting this block meant no check ran at all: adversarial review 2026-09-06 measured that the gate would compare a freshly built C# against an arbitrarily stale Dart snapshot and call it AGREE.

participants.name: csharp
participants.why: the port that was recorded fixed on 2026-09-04 while still returning a silent wrong answer -- the participant this criterion exists to keep honest

freshness.why: a stale binary answers happily, and its answer is about code that is no longer the code -- the 2026-08-13 failure mode
freshness.why_artefacts_not_the_exe: glp_repl.exe is the .NET apphost stub and an incremental build does NOT rewrite it when only a referenced library's method bodies change. Measured 2026-09-06: after editing out/csharp/lib/engine/glp_engine.cs and rebuilding successfully, the exe was 15 minutes older than the assembly carrying the change. The output DIRECTORY's newest file dates the build; the stub dates the launcher.

criteria.script:
${TYPED}/goal_term_acceptance.glp
first_item([send(1,a)], _).
first_item([send(1,_)], Y).
first_item([_], Y).
first_item([send(1,a)], _), first_item([send(2,b)], Z).
first_item([send(1,a)|foo], Y).
first_item([_?], Y).
first_item([send(1,a)], Y).

normalisations.rationale: Both REPLs echo a fixed prompt at the head of a result line. The prompt is line discipline, not a result; it is identical in both and its presence would not distinguish the runtimes anyway. Stripping it keeps the comparison about answers.

negative_control.why: the divergence that matters sits AFTER the prompt. If stripping a fixed prefix could erase a differing binding, every AGREE this rule contributed to would be worthless.

normalisations.rationale: The banner carries the build commit, the compile date and the WORKING DIRECTORY -- and the two participants deliberately run from different working directories (glp_runtime vs the repo root), so the banner differs by construction and would report a permanent false divergence. The retained shapes are exactly the three a goal can answer with: a status line, a binding, or a refusal.
normalisations.declared_limitation: A refusal that did NOT begin with `Error:` would be dropped by this rule and would not be compared. That is a real limitation of the retained set, stated here rather than discovered later; the negative control below pins the three shapes that ARE retained.

negative_control.a:
GLP REPL banner
Working directory: D:\one
→ succeeds
Y = some(send(1, a))
Error: list tail is neither a list nor a variable: foo
negative_control.b:
GLP REPL banner
Working directory: D:\two
→ failed
Y = some(send(2, b))
Error: list tail is neither a list nor a variable: bar
negative_control.why: all three result shapes this criterion can diverge on -- a status, a binding and a refusal -- must survive the filter, and the banner difference the rule exists to remove must not be the only thing left.

rule.pattern: ^Error: list tail is neither a list nor a variable

why: This reproduces the SHAPE of the defect actually measured on 2026-09-04: C# did not
refuse an improper list tail, it silently coerced it to nil and returned the same
answer as the proper-tailed goal. Deleting the refusal line from the C# transcript is
that defect expressed at transcript level. If the comparator cannot see this, it could
not have seen the real one, and this run's MEASURED-AGREE would prove nothing.
Executed on EVERY run against the transcripts captured on that run (FR-007, SC-002).

executed_reversion.what: out/csharp/lib/engine/glp_engine.cs -- the FR-005 improper-tail refusal replaced by the original `tailTerm = new RtConstTerm(null)` coercion, rebuilt, gate run, reverted, rebuilt, gate run again
executed_reversion.why: the in-band negative control above proves the COMPARATOR discriminates. Only reverting the real fix in the real source and rebuilding proves the harness end to end -- runtime, capture, normalisation and comparison -- is a real detector (FR-007, T058). Executed, not asserted.
